lesson.title: The Developer's Mirror: Writing an Honest __repr__
lesson.summary: __repr__ produces an unambiguous, developer-facing description of an object, used by the interactive shell, by the repr() function, and as print()'s fallback when __str__ is missing.
lesson.body:
Open a Python interactive shell and type an expression without printing it, like a list, and Python shows you a value:

```python
>>> [1, 2, 3]
[1, 2, 3]
```

That echoed line does not come from __str__. It comes from __repr__, the method Python calls whenever it needs an unambiguous, precise stand-in for a value, rather than a friendly summary meant for an end user. repr() is a built-in function that calls an object's __repr__ method directly, and the interactive shell calls repr() automatically on whatever expression you evaluate.

The convention, going back to Python's early design, is that a good __repr__ should ideally look like valid Python code that could recreate the object, or at least be unambiguous about exactly what the object is, even if it cannot literally be re-evaluated. Compare these two methods on the same class:

```python
class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Point({self.x}, {self.y})"

    def __str__(self):
        return f"({self.x}, {self.y})"

p = Point(3, 4)
print(p)
print(repr(p))
```

This prints (3, 4) on the first line, from __str__, and Point(3, 4) on the second, from __repr__. The __repr__ version reads like a call to the Point constructor, which is exactly what makes it unambiguous: anyone reading Point(3, 4) in a debugger or a log file knows precisely what type of object they are looking at and what arguments would recreate it.

Now remove __str__ and keep only __repr__:

```python
class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Point({self.x}, {self.y})"

p = Point(3, 4)
print(p)
```

This still prints Point(3, 4), even though print() normally asks for __str__ first. When a class has no __str__ of its own, Python falls back to __repr__ for print() and str() too. This is why many classes only bother defining __repr__: it works everywhere __str__ would, and it also works in the shell and in debuggers, whereas a __str__-only class looks uninformative the moment you inspect it directly in a shell or inside a data structure.

That last point matters more than it first appears. Containers like lists always display their elements using repr(), never str(), even when you print the container itself.

```python
class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Point({self.x}, {self.y})"

    def __str__(self):
        return f"({self.x}, {self.y})"

points = [Point(1, 2), Point(3, 4)]
print(points)
```

This prints [Point(1, 2), Point(3, 4)], using __repr__ for each Point, even though the Point class also defines __str__. Lists do not define their own __str__, so printing a list falls back to its __repr__, exactly the way printing a Point with no __str__ falls back to __repr__ earlier in this chapter, and a list's __repr__ always builds its bracketed text by calling repr(), not str(), on every element it contains. Python's designers made this choice because inside a container, ambiguity is dangerous. If Point's elements displayed as (1, 2) inside a list that also happened to contain real tuples, you would not be able to tell a Point apart from an actual tuple just by reading the output. __repr__ exists to prevent exactly that confusion, which is why writing a good __repr__ for every class you define, even ones that also have __str__, is considered good practice.
